summary: Defines how extensions to the Babel routing protocol are encoded, building on RFC 6126. It lets new features be added without breaking implementations that do not understand them. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 8966.

eli5.summary: A letter format that has room for add-on notes. Readers who do not know the add-on can still read the main letter.

questions: how to extend babel routing protocol
subtitle: A formal scheme to add new features to the Babel routing protocol without breaking old implementations.

tldr.problem: Babel is a routing protocol that needs new features over time, but without a clear extension scheme, different implementations might use the same space in conflicting ways and fail to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC formalizes five extension mechanisms (new protocol versions, new TLVs, sub-TLVs within TLVs, the Flags field, and packet trailers) with clear rules about backward compatibility, so extensions can be added without breaking implementations that do not understand them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7557 was later superseded by RFC 8966, which consolidates Babel protocol specifications.

today: RFC 7557 is an Experimental specification that was later superseded by RFC 8966, which consolidates the Babel routing protocol and its extensions into a single unified specification.

sections.title: Extending the Babel Routing Protocol
sections.content:
Babel is a routing protocol defined in RFC 6126 that routers use to exchange network route information. Like any protocol, Babel needs to evolve to support new features, but there is a challenge: implementations must not break when they receive data they do not understand.

RFC 6126 already includes provisions for this: packets with unknown version numbers, unknown message types (TLVs), and extra data in existing messages are silently ignored by the original protocol. The problem is that without formal rules, independently developed extensions might conflict, using the same extension space in incompatible ways. This RFC formalizes five extension mechanisms with rules designed to ensure extensions remain compatible with old implementations.
sections.eli5: Babel needs to grow, but old routers must still work even when they see new features they don't know about.

sections.title: Five Extension Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC defines five ways to extend Babel, each with specific rules.

Protocol versions: The Babel packet header includes an eight-bit version field. The current version is 2. A future incompatible protocol could use version 3 or higher; implementations receiving an unknown version MUST silently ignore the packet. Versions 0 and 1 were earlier experimental versions and SHOULD NOT be reused.

New TLVs: An extension can define a new TLV (Type-Length-Value) type to carry its data. Unknown TLVs are silently ignored, so this works safely. New TLVs SHOULD be self-terminating (their meaningful length can be determined without knowing their explicit length field) and any extra data in them SHOULD be structured as sub-TLVs. TLV types 224 through 254 are reserved for experimental use; type 255 is reserved for future expansion.

Sub-TLVs: Many Babel TLVs are self-terminating, meaning their meaningful length is smaller than their explicit length. Extensions can store data in the extra space as sub-TLVs, which need not be self-terminating. Sub-TLVs have their own type and length fields and are interpreted based on which TLV contains them. Sub-TLV types 224–254 are for experimental use; type 255 is reserved for expansion.

Flags field: The Update TLV contains an eight-bit Flags field. Bits 0 and 1 are defined by the original protocol; the remaining six bits are undefined and silently ignored. Due to limited space, using flags is NOT RECOMMENDED; a sub-TLV is preferred.

Packet trailer: A Babel packet fits inside a UDP datagram, which may have extra space. The extra data at the end (the packet trailer) is silently ignored. Originally intended for cryptographic trailers, no currently deployed extension uses it, so its format remains undefined.
sections.eli5: Extensions can add a new version number, new message types, extra data within messages, new flag bits, or trailing data—each with backward-compatible rules.

sections.title: Sub-TLV Format and Structure
sections.content:
Sub-TLVs use the same structure as TLVs: a Type byte, a Length byte, and a Body. Except for the special Pad1 type (which is just a single zero byte), all sub-TLVs have these three fields.

Two sub-TLVs are defined by this document for padding: Pad1 (type 0) and PadN (type 1). Pad1 is a single zero byte used to fill one byte; PadN includes a length and a body of zero bytes, allowing padding of any length. Both are silently ignored on reception. Unknown sub-TLVs MUST also be silently ignored by implementations that use sub-TLVs.

The interpretation of a sub-TLV type can depend on which TLV contains it, allowing the same sub-TLV type number to mean different things in different contexts.
sections.eli5: Sub-TLVs are tiny messages within messages, with type and length fields. Some are for padding, and unknown ones are always ignored.

sections.title: Choosing Among Extension Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC provides guidance on which mechanism to use for a given extension.

New versions should only be used when the new version is not backwards compatible with the original protocol, since defining a new version breaks compatibility with old implementations.

New TLVs vs. sub-TLVs: Both can carry extension data. When an old implementation sees an unknown TLV, it ignores the entire TLV and cannot act on it. When it sees a known TLV with unknown sub-TLVs, it parses and acts on the known TLV and silently ignores the unknown sub-TLVs. A sub-TLV should be used when the extension is compatible with the meaning of the TLV it is attached to (the extension data is optional). A new TLV must be used when the extension fundamentally changes the TLV's meaning and should not be acted upon by old implementations that do not understand it.

Flags field: Using a bit in the Flags field saves space compared to a sub-TLV, but the available space is tiny (only 6 bits). Due to space constraints and small savings, a sub-TLV is recommended instead.

Packet trailer: Due to lack of implementation experience, no recommendations are made about its use.
sections.eli5: Use new versions rarely, new TLVs when meaning changes fundamentally, sub-TLVs for compatible add-ons, and generally avoid flags.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Interoperability
sections.content:
The RFC establishes three IANA registries to coordinate extension assignments: one for TLV types, one for sub-TLV types, and one for Flags values. The allocation policy is Specification Required, meaning any extension type must be assigned by IANA after publication of a specification.

For each registry, the RFC provides initial values. The TLV types include the original types from RFC 6126 (Pad1, Hello, Update, etc.) plus entries from related extensions like source-specific routing and HMAC authentication. Types 224–254 are reserved for Experimental Use, and type 255 is reserved for future expansion of the type space.

By centralizing these registries, the RFC ensures that no two independently developed extensions accidentally use the same type numbers and conflict with each other, maintaining interoperability across implementations.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps official lists of type numbers for extensions, preventing conflicts and ensuring different Babel implementations can work together.
